To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the internationally optimal emission permit levels are lower than the nationally optimal permit levels and that the internationally optimal permit levels are lower the larger the difference in external balances between the countries.
the internationally optimal emission permit levels are not necessarily equal and may be lower than the nationally optimal permit levels.
the Nash equilibrium is inefficient and that the Nash equilibrium permit levels can either be increased or reduced in order to achieve efficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a two-country overlapping generation model in which the environment is a global public good and national emission permit systems are in place.
the effects of national emission permit systems on the international allocation of emission permits and the environment.

the question of how the national emission permit levels in two countries are determined when each government maximizes national economic and environmental welfare, and the environment is a global public good.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the internationally optimal emission permit levels are either higher than the nationally optimal ones or lower or equal, depending on the direction and size of the countries’ external balances and their relative environmental preferences.
the nationally optimal permit levels are not internationally optimal.
the nationally optimal permit level in one country should be adjusted in a certain direction if and only if the other country’s permit level should be adjusted in the same direction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a globally coordinated permit system is needed in order to achieve Pareto efficient permit levels.

the internationally optimal permit level is lower than the nationally optimal one, and that the internationally optimal level is lower than that of the country with the lower environmental preferences.
the international coordination of emission permits would improve the economic and environmental performance of the two countries and would also reduce the net foreign debt of the debtor country.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when national permit systems and global public good provision interact in a world of asymmetric countries, national policies may be inefficient.

, in the absence of a global emission permit system, the direction and size of the adjustment to nationally optimal emission permit levels required for international efficiency depends on the direction and size, respectively, of differences between countries in their external balances and environmental policy objectives.
international cooperation in the form of permit trading can be a Pareto improving policy option.
